title: Corvina
description: Valpolicella's leading grape: cherry-fresh when young, rich and raisined as Amarone.
L: Corvina, or Corvina Veronese, is the main grape of Valpolicella, near Verona. On its own, it gives light to medium-bodied wines with sour cherry, red berries, almond and herbs. Colour is moderate, tannins are low, acidity is fresh. It's a very different wine before and after drying.

Corvina has thick skins, loose bunches and good resistance to rot, which make it ideal for drying grapes after harvest. During drying, it develops a compound profile rich in aromatic precursors, and its skins help resist mould. That's why it's the backbone of Amarone and Recioto.
Thick skins and loose bunches for drying
Why is Corvina well suited to drying?
Thick skins and loose bunches that resist rot
Loose bunches let air circulate, and thick skins resist mould during months of drying.

A simple Valpolicella is pale to medium ruby, with bright cherry and a slightly bitter almond finish. Amarone is deep, with dried cherry, raisin, chocolate and spice, and high alcohol. That bitter cherry and almond note links them all.
Cherry with a bitter almond finish
Corvina naturally gives deep-coloured, very tannic wines.
Not true. Fresh Corvina is moderately coloured with low tannin. Drying gives Amarone its concentration.
Corvina gives sour cherry, almond and fresh acidity
Thick skins and loose bunches make it ideal for drying
Valpolicella's styles all share its cherry and almond

Corvina grows almost only in the Veneto, around Verona. Valpolicella lies north of the city, in valleys running down from the Lessini mountains. The Classico zone, the historic heart, has valleys like Fumane, Marano and Negrar. Valpantena and the eastern zone extend it. Bardolino, on Lake Garda, also uses Corvina.

Valpolicella wines must be 45 to 95% Corvina, with Corvinone, a separate, larger-berried grape, allowed to replace up to half of it. Rondinella adds colour and resistance; Molinara, once common, adds acidity but is now less used. Oseleta, an old local grape, is being revived for its colour and tannin.
Match each grape to its role.
Valpolicella is a blend led by Corvina.
Bardolino, from Corvina on Lake Garda's shores, is lighter than Valpolicella. Its rosé, Chiaretto, is one of Italy's best pink wines.
Valpolicella must contain between 45 and ____% Corvina.
Producers can use 45 to 95% Corvina, with Corvinone replacing up to half.
Corvina grows around Verona, in Valpolicella and Bardolino
Valpolicella blends Corvina with Corvinone and Rondinella
The Classico zone is the historic heart
Explain how drying changes the grape

Appassimento is the drying of grapes after harvest. Healthy, loose bunches are picked by hand and laid on bamboo racks or plastic crates in airy lofts, called fruttai. They dry for about 100 to 120 days, losing 30 to 40% of their weight. Sugar, acid and flavour concentrate.
Three to four months in fruttai

Drying is a living process. The berries keep metabolising, changing their chemistry. Some acids decrease, glycerol rises, and new aromas form. Resveratrol and other compounds increase. A little noble rot sometimes develops, adding complexity. The result is dried cherry, raisin and spice flavours.
Grapes keep living as they dry
How much weight do grapes typically lose during appassimento?
About a third, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour.

Traditionally, grapes dried in attics with open windows, at the mercy of the weather. Today many fruttai have fans and dehumidifiers to control conditions and prevent grey rot. Some producers argue that natural drying gives more complexity; others prefer control. Both are allowed.
Fermentation happens after drying, not during.
Appassimento dries grapes for three to four months
Berries lose 30 to 40% of their weight and change chemically
Modern lofts control humidity to prevent rot

Recioto della Valpolicella is the oldest style: dried grapes fermented to leave sweetness. Amarone della Valpolicella, DOCG since 2010, is fermented almost dry, reaching 15 to 16% alcohol. Amarone means the big bitter one, compared with Recioto's sweetness. Legend says it was born when a Recioto fermented too far.

Ripasso, meaning re-passed, is made by refermenting young Valpolicella on the leftover skins of Amarone or Recioto. The skins add sugar, colour, tannin and dried fruit flavour, plus a few degrees of alcohol. The result sits between simple Valpolicella and Amarone, sometimes called baby Amarone.
Put the steps of making a Ripasso in order.
Ripasso borrows the skins left after Amarone is pressed, so Amarone comes first.

Amarone must age at least two years from January after harvest; Riserva at least four. Traditionally, it aged in large Slavonian oak casks; many producers now use French barriques. Producers like Quintarelli and Dal Forno made it famous worldwide.
By drying grapes for six months
By refermenting Valpolicella on Amarone skins
The leftover skins add body and flavour.
Recioto is sweet; Amarone is dry and powerful, at 15 to 16%
Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on Amarone skins
Amarone ages at least two years; Riserva four
Pair each Valpolicella style with food

Light Valpolicella suits salumi, pizza and pasta, served slightly cool. Ripasso suits risotto, roast meats and polenta. Amarone suits braised beef, game, aged Parmigiano and Monte Veronese cheese; in Verona it flavours risotto all'Amarone. Recioto goes with dark chocolate and dry pastries.
Light to rich, starter to dessert

Serve Valpolicella at 14 to 16 degrees, Ripasso and Amarone at 16 to 18, Recioto slightly cooler. Valpolicella is best within three years; Ripasso within eight; Amarone ages 10 to 25 years. Decant young Amarone for its power and alcohol.
Match each wine to a pairing.
Corvina offers a wine for each course.
Amarone is high in alcohol. Serve it in a large glass, not too warm, and give it time to open.
Amarone can age for 10 to 25 years.
Yes. Its concentration, alcohol and structure help it age.
Valpolicella suits everyday food; Amarone rich dishes
Serve Amarone at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted
Match each wine to its making.
The airy loft where grapes dry for appassimento.
Amarone means the big bitter one.
Which grapes are used in Valpolicella blends?
During appassimento grapes lose about 30 to ____% of their weight.
About a third of their weight, concentrating sugar and flavour.
Corvina gives cherry, almond and freshness
Its thick skins and loose bunches suit drying
Amarone, Recioto and Ripasso come from appassimento
